subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What is meant by the term 'urbanisation'?
options: The increase in the proportion of a population living in towns and cities
The movement of people from cities to the countryside
The decline of industry in city centres
The redevelopment of derelict inner-city land
questions.explain: Urbanisation is the growth in the proportion of a country's population that lives in urban areas.

questions.q: Which of the following is a 'push' factor encouraging people to leave rural areas?
options: Lack of employment and poor services
Better healthcare in the city
More entertainment and shops
Higher wages in urban factories
questions.explain: Push factors are negative conditions, such as unemployment and poor services, that drive people away from an area.

questions.q: Which of the following is a 'pull' factor attracting people to urban areas?
options: Greater availability of jobs and services
Drought and crop failure
Rural isolation
Lack of schools in the countryside
questions.explain: Pull factors are positive attractions, such as more jobs and better services, that draw people towards a place.

questions.q: Why do many LEDCs experience very rapid urban growth?
options: High rates of rural-urban migration combined with natural increase
People moving out of cities to the countryside
Falling birth rates in cities
Government policies that restrict city size
questions.explain: Rapid urban growth in LEDCs is driven mainly by rural-urban migration alongside natural increase in the cities.

questions.q: What does the term 'rural-urban migration' describe?
options: The movement of people from the countryside to towns and cities
The movement of people between two different cities
The growth of cities outwards into the countryside
The return of people from cities to rural villages
questions.explain: Rural-urban migration is the movement of people from rural areas into urban areas.

questions.q: How does 'natural increase' add to the population of a city?
options: The number of births exceeds the number of deaths
More people move in than move out
The city boundary is extended outwards
New towns are built nearby
questions.explain: Natural increase occurs when births outnumber deaths, raising the population without any migration.

questions.q: In the Burgess urban land-use model, how are the zones arranged around the city centre?
options: As concentric rings
As wedges or sectors
In a random scatter
In a linear strip
questions.explain: The Burgess model shows land use as concentric rings expanding outwards from the central business district.

questions.q: How does the Hoyt model differ from the Burgess model in showing urban land use?
options: Land use forms sectors or wedges, often along transport routes
Land use forms perfect concentric circles
There is no central business district
All housing is of the same type
questions.explain: The Hoyt model arranges land use in sectors that develop outwards along major transport routes.

questions.q: What do the letters 'CBD' stand for in urban geography?
options: Central Business District
City Border Development
Central Bypass District
Commercial Building Division
questions.explain: The CBD is the Central Business District, the commercial heart of a town or city.

questions.q: Why does the CBD typically have the highest land values in a city?
options: It is the most accessible and central location
It contains the oldest terraced housing
It has the largest amount of open green space
It is furthest from public transport
questions.explain: High accessibility and competition for a central site push land values to their highest in the CBD.

questions.q: Which feature is most typical of the traditional inner-city zone?
options: Older, high-density terraced housing and former industry
Large detached houses with big gardens
Out-of-town retail parks
Modern glass office towers
questions.explain: The inner city is characterised by older, densely packed terraced housing built near former industrial areas.

questions.q: What does the term 'counter-urbanisation' mean?
options: The movement of people out of cities into rural or semi-rural areas
The rapid growth of city centres
The building of new office towers in the CBD
The migration of people from villages into cities
questions.explain: Counter-urbanisation is the movement of people away from large urban areas towards smaller settlements and the countryside.

questions.q: What is 'suburbanisation'?
options: The outward growth of a city as people move to housing on its edges
The redevelopment of derelict CBD sites
The decline of population in rural villages
The concentration of industry in the inner city
questions.explain: Suburbanisation is the spread of a city outwards as people move to housing in the suburbs on its margins.

questions.q: A developer wants to build a large department store where it will attract the most customers and be easiest to reach by public transport. Where in the city is this land likely to be found?
options: In the CBD, where land is most accessible
On the rural-urban fringe, far from bus routes
In the inner-city terraced housing zone
In a quiet residential suburb
questions.explain: The CBD offers maximum accessibility and footfall, making it the prime location for a large retail store.

questions.q: What is one common impact of building large out-of-town shopping centres?
options: A decline in trade and shops within the traditional CBD
An increase in the number of independent shops in the CBD
A fall in the use of cars for shopping trips
A rise in the population of inner-city terraces
questions.explain: Out-of-town retailing draws shoppers away from the city centre, often leading to CBD decline and shop closures.

questions.q: What is an 'ecological footprint'?
options: The area of land and water needed to supply a population's resources and absorb its waste
The total number of parks within a city
The amount of derelict land in the inner city
The distance people travel to work each day
questions.explain: An ecological footprint measures the area of land and water required to provide resources and absorb the waste of a population.

questions.q: Which of the following would help to make a city more sustainable?
options: Increasing recycling and using renewable energy sources
Encouraging greater use of private cars
Sending all waste to landfill
Removing green spaces to build more roads
questions.explain: Recycling and renewable energy reduce resource use and waste, lowering a city's ecological footprint.

questions.q: A city council wants to reduce traffic congestion and air pollution in a sustainable way. Which measure best achieves this?
options: Investing in an efficient public transport and cycling network
Building more multi-storey car parks in the CBD
Widening motorways into the city centre
Reducing bus services to save money
questions.explain: Better public transport and cycling encourage people to leave cars at home, cutting congestion and pollution.

questions.q: A planner includes parks and tree-lined streets in a new urban development. Which benefit best supports sustainability?
options: Green spaces improve air quality and provide habitats for wildlife
Green spaces increase the amount of traffic
Green spaces raise the city's ecological footprint
Green spaces reduce the need for recycling schemes
questions.explain: Green spaces absorb pollutants, support biodiversity and improve quality of life, all of which aid sustainability.

questions.q: Why is reducing, reusing and recycling waste important in a sustainable city?
options: It conserves resources and cuts the amount of waste sent to landfill
It increases the demand for raw materials
It encourages more use of private cars
It expands the city's ecological footprint
questions.explain: Managing waste through the three Rs conserves natural resources and reduces landfill, lowering environmental impact.
